passages.happening:
David leaves Gath and takes refuge in the cave of Adullam. His brothers and his father's household come down to him there (verse 1). “And all who were distressed or indebted or discontented rallied around him, and he became their leader. About four hundred men were with him” (verse 2).

David goes to Mizpeh in Moab and asks the king of Moab to let his father and mother stay there ‘until I learn what God will do for me’ (verse 3). They stay with the king of Moab the whole time David is in the stronghold (verse 4).

Then the prophet Gad tells David not to stay in the stronghold but to go into the land of Judah, and David goes to the forest of Hereth (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
In the last chapter David was alone, hungry, and pretending to be mad among the Philistines. Now two kingdoms are taking shape. Around David gather outcasts, a prophet, and by the end of the chapter a priest. Around Saul gather suspicion, informers and a foreign killer.

Adullam was a town in the lowlands of Judah, southwest of Bethlehem, not far from the Valley of Elah, in country full of limestone caves.

The men who come to David are described by their troubles: people under pressure, people in debt, people bitter in spirit. In the ancient world such people often left settled life and formed bands on the edges, living by raiding or by hiring themselves out for protection. David's band follows that pattern, but under him it becomes the heart of a future royal army. God's people have often been formed from the margins rather than the center.

Moab lay east of the Dead Sea. David's choice of it as a refuge for his parents makes sense. According to the book of Ruth, his great-grandmother Ruth was a Moabite. It may also reflect Moab's hostility toward Saul, who had fought against it.

The stronghold was a natural fortress in rough country, not a built castle. Gad the prophet appears here for the first time. He will serve David when David is king.
passages.later:
Two psalm headings set their prayers in a cave: ‘A Maskil of David, when he was in the cave. A prayer’ (Psalm 142:1), and ‘A Miktam of David, when he fled from Saul into the cave’ (Psalm 57:1). The headings do not say which cave, this one or the one at En-gedi in chapter 24.

Gad served David to the end of his reign. Years later he is called ‘Gad the prophet, David’s seer’ (2 Samuel 24:11).
passages.asks: The distressed, the indebted and the bitter came to David, and he became their leader. Ask who in your community has nowhere else to go, and whether they would find a welcome with you. And if you are one of them, ask what it would mean to come to the one God has chosen.

passages.happening:
Saul hears that David has been found. He is sitting under the tamarisk tree on the hill at Gibeah, spear in hand, his servants standing around him (verse 6). “Listen, men of Benjamin! Is the son of Jesse giving all of you fields and vineyards and making you commanders of thousands or hundreds?” (verse 7). He accuses them all of conspiring against him, and of hiding his own son's covenant with David (verse 8).

Doeg the Edomite speaks up. He saw David come to Ahimelech at Nob. The priest asked the LORD for him, gave him food, and gave him Goliath's sword (verses 9-10).

Saul summons Ahimelech and all the priests of his family. He accuses Ahimelech of conspiring with David (verses 11-13). Ahimelech answers, “Who among all your servants is as faithful as David, the king’s son-in-law, the captain of your bodyguard who is honored in your house?” (verse 14). He knew nothing of any quarrel, he says.

Saul answers with a sentence of death: “You will surely die, Ahimelech, you and all your father’s house!” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The chapter moves back and forth between David and Saul, and the pictures are drawn with care. Saul sits under a tree with a spear in his hand, surrounded by servants he suspects. David stands in a cave, surrounded by people who have nowhere else to go.

Saul's speech appeals to tribal loyalty. He calls them men of Benjamin, his own tribe, and asks whether David, a man of Judah, would give them fields and commands as Saul has. Gifts of land and posts in the army were how ancient kings kept loyalty.

Saul uses the word conspire twice. He sees plots everywhere. The text shows that no one is plotting against him.

Ahimelech asks who is as faithful as David. The word comes from the root of amen. It is the truest thing said before Saul in the whole chapter, and Saul answers it with a death sentence.
passages.later: The heading of Psalm 52 sets that psalm here, ‘After Doeg the Edomite went to Saul and told him’ that David had gone to Ahimelech's house. The psalm begins, ‘Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man?’ (Psalm 52:1).
passages.asks: Ahimelech told the king the truth about David, and it cost him his life. Ask when telling the truth about someone has cost you, or would. And ask whether, like Saul, you see plots against you that are not there.

passages.t: The priests of Nob, and the one who escaped
passages.happening:
Saul orders his guards to kill the priests of the LORD, ‘But the king’s servants would not lift a hand to strike the priests of the LORD’ (verse 17). So he orders Doeg, and Doeg kills them himself, eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod (verse 18). Then he strikes Nob, the town of the priests, with its men and women, children and infants, and its animals (verse 19).

One son of Ahimelech escapes, Abiathar, and he flees to David and tells him what Saul has done (verses 20-21).

David answers, “I knew that Doeg the Edomite was there that day, and that he was sure to tell Saul. I myself am responsible for the lives of everyone in your father’s house” (verse 22). “Stay with me; do not be afraid, for he who seeks your life is seeking mine as well. You will be safe with me” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Killing priests was a shocking act. Saul's own guards refuse, and he has to turn to a foreigner.

The list in verse 19, men and women, children and infants, is the same list as the command about Amalek in chapter 15. Saul carries out against the priests of the LORD the total destruction he failed to carry out against Amalek. The rejected king has turned his sword on God's own servants.

The massacre fulfills the word spoken long before against Eli's house (2:31-33), since the priests of Nob were Eli's descendants. Yet the chapter puts the guilt squarely on Saul and Doeg.

David does not excuse himself. He says plainly that his lie at Nob cost these lives. Then he takes the survivor into his care: Abiathar will be safe with him. In the next chapter Abiathar will bring the ephod, and the priest of the house of Eli will serve the anointed king.
passages.later:
The last part of the word against Eli's house came true under Solomon, when Abiathar was removed from the priesthood (1 Kings 2:27).

The prophets insist that each person answers for his own sin: “A son will not bear the iniquity of his father, and a father will not bear the iniquity of his son” (Ezekiel 18:20).
passages.hard:
Why did God allow the innocent priests of Nob and their families to be slaughtered?

The chapter does not soften this atrocity or offer an easy explanation. Several things can be said. The text puts the guilt squarely on Saul and Doeg, and through David's own words it admits his part. It also recalls the judgment long announced on Eli's house, which suggests that God's purposes were at work even in this evil, without making the killers any less guilty.

Some readers find that framework troubling, since the dead include children who had no part in Eli's sins. Others note that the Old Testament often speaks of consequences falling on families and communities, while it also insists that each person is judged for his own sin.

The chapter's own response is lament and protection. David takes responsibility and shelters the survivor. It does not ask the reader to call the slaughter good.

A word of care. This story must not be used to say that a sudden death, an accident or an illness today is God's punishment on the person who suffered it. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning: of people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you have lost someone suddenly, or carry fear or guilt after reading this, please speak with someone you trust, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: David said, ‘I myself am responsible.’ Ask whether there is harm you have caused that you have not yet owned. And ask whom you could shelter, as David sheltered Abiathar, because your failure helped to put them in danger.
